page.text_excerpt: Blog Games Projects Dominic Szablewski, @phoboslab — Tuesday, November 3rd 2026 Why this Obscure Audio Codec is a Perfect Fit for the N64 Sorry for the clickbait title. I promise this post delivers: 44100 Hz stereo with near-Opus bitrates using about 4% of the N64’s CPU time. But first, some history: The options for playing and storing audio data on the N64 were dire. The PlayStation could just stream uncompressed redbook audio straight from the CD. On the N64, cartridge space was at a premium and time on the 93 MHz CPU was limited. Worse, access to the vector co-processor, the RSP, was guarded by Nintendo for the longest time. Nintendo's own platform library, Libultra, internally used the RSP for various graphics and sound-related tasks, but Nintendo didn't allow third-party developers to directly write code for it. Libultra provided some functions to transparently play back compressed audio using an ADPCM scheme (adaptive differential pulse code modulation). The RSP handled decompression on the fly, just before the audio was sent to the output buffer. This works well enough and cuts the space needed for a sample by a factor of 4. Still, a 5-minute stereo audio track at 44100 Hz will land at about 12MB – way too much for an N64 cartridge, even when you cut the sample rate in half. The whole Mario 64 ROM is just 8MB in total. The biggest N64 games were 64MB. So N64 games produced music similarly to a tracker: short samples were scheduled and played back with some limited effects at the right time. With the space constraints on the cartridge, fully “recorded” audio was pretty much out of the question. Later in the N64's life, some blessed developers were allowed by Nintendo to directly access the RSP. Most famously, Conker's Bad Fur Day used this to decompress MP3 audio for the myriad of speech samples in the game. Decoding MP3 is quite expensive and the frame rate of the game suffered. page.title: Organizing Intelligence
page.description: When will advances in AI lead to economic transformation? We develop a model of how intelligence, the ability to achieve goals, matters for organizations, the key unit of economic production. Agents (human or AI) with multidimensional capabilities sort endogenously into competing firms. A firm's productivity depends on its agents' capabilities; we distinguish competence, which shifts productivity levels, from coordination, which governs how productivity scales with size. Two differences between AI and humans drive transformation: AI expertise is reproducible while humans' are in fixed supply, and AIs may not face the same human limits on coordination. We analyze how equilibrium market structure, productivity, employment, and wages evolve as AI capabilities improve. When AI is more capable than the average human, organizations of complementary humans can nonetheless outperform AI. Increases in AI competence can change the composition of workers within firms and decrease firm size. As AI coordination improves, however, this can break the Coasean ceiling on firm size and the market structure undergoes a phase transition toward large, concentrated AI-heavy firms. Changes in human employment are gradual when AI displaces workers within mixed human-AI firms, or sudden when AI firms outcompete human firms. We decompose wage changes into a technology effect, which changes the value of humans within existing firms, and a reorganization effect as firms adjust size and composition. Reorganization can reverse the technology effect on wages.

Read more → Words by Samuel Hughes Did medieval people love their children? 21st July 2026 5 Mins Is it really plausible that children survived the hardship of medieval life without devoted parents? Growing up, I acquired a vague idea that medieval people did not view childhood as we do. I was told they saw children merely as defective or incomplete adults, and that they did not love their children as we love ours, perhaps as a way of coping with high infant mortality. As I grew older, I came to associate this idea with the name of Philippe Ariès, a French historian who argued in the 1960s that medieval childhood was profoundly remote in these ways. Ariès’s work never attained complete acceptance in academia, but it was vastly influential on the wider public. As it turns out, however, Ariès’s view is just not true. This has been established beyond doubt by a wealth of later scholarship across Europe. Nicholas Orme’s Medieval Children is the leading study for England in particular. ‘It cannot be overemphasised that there is nothing to be said for Ariès’s view,’ Orme notes. It is mistaken ‘not simply in detail but in substance. It is time to lay it to rest.’ The Works in Progress Newsletter Get new articles from Works in Progress delivered to your inbox. page.text_excerpt: Apple Store Mac iPad iPhone Watch Vision AirPods Home Entertainment Accessories Support 0 + About the illuminated Apple logo on MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display includes an illuminated Apple logo on the back of its display. How Apple logo illumination works The Apple logo behind the built-in display is illuminated whenever the Mac is awake. It automatically dims or brightens based on the brightness level of the built-in screen and the lighting conditions detected by the computer’s ambient light sensor. For all screen-brightness levels, the Apple logo will be dimmer in a dim room and brighter in a bright room. How to turn off Apple logo illumination Requires MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display To make the Apple logo dark in all lighting conditions, you can turn off its illumination using Terminal, which is in the Utilities folder of your Applications folder. You can also use Spotlight to find and open it. Type or paste this command in Terminal, then press Return: sudo defaults write com.apple.CoreBrightness LEBacklightMode -int 0 Type your administrator password when prompted (Terminal doesn’t show the password as it's typed), then press Return. Logo illumination turns off immediately. This change affects all macOS user accounts, including when starting up from macOS Recovery. When migrating to a new Mac, the setting transfers to the new Mac. How to turn Apple logo illumination back on To turn logo illumination on again, enter this command in Terminal: sudo defaults delete com.apple.CoreBrightness LEBacklightMode Reinstalling macOS also turns illumination back on.
